consultation: Your first consultation is always free — a 30–45 minute call to review your situation. In-person and secure Zoom meetings available.

items.q: When should I contact an attorney about a board complaint?
items.a: As soon as possible — ideally before you respond to the board at all. You always have more options the earlier you start, and the initial consultation with Craig K. Perry is free. If you've received a Notice of Investigation, the board typically expects a response within 14 days.

items.q: Do I have to self-report to my licensing board?
items.a: It depends on your license type, the nature of the issue, and the specific circumstances. Self-reporting can carry real consequences and should not be done without first consulting an attorney. We can help you determine your obligations and how to respond strategically.

items.q: What happens at a disciplinary hearing?
items.a: A disciplinary hearing is an administrative proceeding before your licensing board. You have the right to be represented by an attorney, to present evidence, and to cross-examine witnesses. The outcome can range from a reprimand or fine to license suspension or revocation. Having experienced legal representation significantly improves your odds.

items.q: Can I keep practicing while under investigation?
items.a: Usually yes — a license investigation does not automatically suspend your license. However, the board can seek an emergency suspension in serious cases. Contact us immediately if you receive any communication from your licensing board.

items.q: How long does a board investigation take?
items.a: It varies widely — from a few months to over a year, depending on the complexity of the case and the board involved. Some matters can be resolved quickly through informal conferences; others proceed to formal hearings. We'll give you a realistic picture of your timeline at the outset.

items.q: What does it cost to hire Craig K. Perry?
items.a: Fees vary by case complexity. The initial consultation is always free. We'll discuss fee structures at that consultation — including whether a flat fee, retainer, or other arrangement makes sense for your situation.

items.q: My malpractice insurer assigned me an attorney — do I still need my own?
items.a: It depends. Malpractice defense attorneys represent your insurer's interests, which may not align perfectly with yours — particularly when it comes to your license. A separate attorney focused on your license defense can be critical, especially if the board investigation parallels a civil case.

items.q: Can a revoked or surrendered license be reinstated?
items.a: Often yes. After a specified period (which varies by board and by the nature of the original action), you may petition for reinstatement. We can help you build the strongest possible case for returning to practice.

items.q: Can a Nevada licensing board suspend my license before a hearing?
items.a: Yes, in limited cases. Under NRS 233B.127, a board can order an emergency (summary) suspension when it finds that public health, safety, or welfare requires immediate action. A prompt hearing must follow. Most investigations do not involve a summary suspension.

items.q: Is a Notice of Investigation the same as discipline?
items.a: No. An investigation is not discipline, and many investigations end in dismissal or a non-disciplinary letter. How you respond at this stage strongly affects whether the case goes further.

items.q: Do I have to tell my employer about a board investigation?
items.a: It depends on your license, your employment contract, and facility policies. Some obligations are mandatory; others are not. Ask your attorney before disclosing.

items.q: Will board discipline show up publicly?
items.a: Formal discipline is generally public and appears on the board's license lookup. Dismissals and many non-disciplinary outcomes are not. Health-care discipline is also typically reported to the National Practitioner Data Bank.

items.q: How long does the Nevada board discipline process take?
items.a: Anywhere from a few months to more than a year, depending on the board, the complexity of the allegations, expert review, and whether the case settles or goes to hearing.

items.q: Will I be criminally charged for drug diversion in Nevada?
items.a: Not necessarily. Many diversion cases are handled only by the licensing board. But boards and employers can refer cases to law enforcement, so anything you say should be treated as if it could be used in a criminal case.

items.q: Can I keep my license after a diversion allegation?
items.a: Often, yes. Outcomes range from dismissal to monitoring agreements, probation, suspension, or revocation. Early representation and a well-documented response make a significant difference.

items.q: Should I agree to a substance-use evaluation?
items.a: Talk to your attorney first. Who performs the evaluation, what records they see, and how the results are used all matter.

items.q: Can the Nevada board investigate me based only on PMP data?
items.a: Yes. PMP data can prompt an investigation on its own, but data alone doesn't prove improper prescribing — documentation and expert review do.

items.q: Does the Board of Pharmacy have authority over physicians?
items.a: It can regulate practitioners who dispense or hold controlled-substance registrations in Nevada, in addition to the practitioner's own board.

items.q: What happens after an expert reviews my charts?
items.a: If the expert finds no violation, cases often close. If the expert criticizes care, you can respond with your own expert and argument before the board decides whether to file charges.

items.q: Will a positive drug test end my career?
items.a: Usually not. Many professionals complete evaluation and monitoring and continue practicing. How the case is handled early matters a great deal.

items.q: Is a monitoring program public discipline?
items.a: It depends on the board and how the agreement is structured. Some arrangements can be non-public; others are formal discipline.

items.q: What if my prescribed medication caused the positive result?
items.a: Provide documentation through your attorney. Medical review of the result can show a legitimate prescription.

items.q: What happens if I miss a random drug test on probation?
items.a: It is usually treated as a violation and can be treated like a positive test. Outcomes range from a warning to suspension, depending on your history and explanation.

items.q: What is a dilute test and why does it matter?
items.a: A dilute specimen has low concentration and may be treated as suspicious. Medical explanations, such as hydration or certain conditions, can matter.

items.q: Can my probation be extended instead of my license suspended?
items.a: Often yes. Renegotiated terms, including longer probation, are a common resolution for many violations.

items.q: Can I lose my Nevada nursing license for legal marijuana use?
items.a: Legal off-duty use alone is not usually grounds for discipline, but a positive test can lead to employer action and a board inquiry. Use while on probation or monitoring can be a violation.

items.q: Can trace amounts of THC cost me my job?
items.a: Yes. Employment may still be jeopardized even without evidence of impairment, depending on the employer's policy.

items.q: What about CBD?
items.a: Some CBD products contain THC and can cause a positive test. Keep product documentation and get advice.

items.q: Does a malpractice settlement mean the board will discipline me?
items.a: No. Settlements can trigger review, but boards make their own judgment about the care, and many reviews close without discipline.

items.q: Do I need a separate lawyer if my insurer gave me one?
items.a: Often, yes. The insurer's lawyer is focused on the civil claim. A license defense lawyer focuses on keeping your license and record clean.

items.q: Who decides if I met the standard of care?
items.a: Usually an expert reviewer in your field advises the board. You can submit your own expert opinion in response.

items.q: Can an RN perform Botox or filler injections in Nevada?
items.a: Only within the limits of Nevada law, the nurse's license, and proper physician or APRN orders and supervision. Med spa arrangements frequently fall short — get advice before taking on aesthetic work.

items.q: My employer told me to do it. Am I still responsible?
items.a: You can be. Boards hold each licensee responsible for staying within their own scope, but the employer's direction is important context in your defense.

items.q: Is a scope complaint always public discipline?
items.a: No. Many are resolved with education or a non-disciplinary outcome, especially when the licensee responds well early.

items.q: Can an abuse allegation lead to emergency suspension?
items.a: Yes, if the board believes there is an immediate risk to patients. Most cases do not involve emergency suspension, but early representation is critical.

items.q: What if the allegation comes from a confused patient?
items.a: The board must still investigate, but reliability of the account, corroboration, and records matter a great deal to the outcome.

items.q: Is neglect different from abuse?
items.a: Yes. Neglect usually involves failure to provide required care, often tied to staffing and workload, while abuse involves intentional harmful conduct.

items.q: Is a charting mistake grounds for discipline in Nevada?
items.a: It can be, but boards distinguish isolated errors from patterns and from intentional falsification. Many honest errors resolve without public discipline.

items.q: Can I add a late entry to fix a chart?
items.a: Only following your facility's late-entry policy, clearly labeled and dated, and never after you learn of a complaint without legal advice.

items.q: Why does 'dishonesty' matter so much?
items.a: Boards view dishonesty as a character issue that goes to fitness to practice, so it can lead to harsher discipline than the clinical issue itself.

items.q: Can a HIPAA violation cost me my Nevada license?
items.a: It can lead to discipline for unprofessional conduct, though most privacy cases result in lesser outcomes such as reprimands or education, especially for first-time, non-malicious conduct.

items.q: I looked up my own chart. Is that a violation?
items.a: Many employers prohibit it unless done through the patient portal. It's usually treated less seriously than accessing others' records, but it can still lead to discipline.

items.q: Does the Nevada board enforce HIPAA?
items.a: No — federal regulators enforce HIPAA. But the board can discipline the same conduct as unprofessional conduct under your licensing statute.

items.q: Can billing errors lead to license discipline in Nevada?
items.a: Yes, especially if the board finds dishonesty. Honest errors with corrective action usually fare much better.

items.q: Should I wait until the criminal case is over?
items.a: No. License strategy should be coordinated from the start, because statements in one case can affect the others.

items.q: Does repayment end the board case?
items.a: Not automatically, but repayment and corrective action can significantly improve the license outcome.

items.q: Do I have to report a DUI arrest to my Nevada licensing board?
items.a: It depends on your board and whether it is an arrest, charge, or conviction. Some reporting is triggered only by conviction or on renewal. Get advice for your specific license before reporting.

items.q: Can a DUI cost me my nursing or medical license in Nevada?
items.a: A single DUI rarely leads to revocation on its own, but it can lead to an investigation, evaluation, or monitoring, especially if there are signs of substance-use disorder or it is not disclosed.

items.q: What if I didn't disclose an old conviction on my application?
items.a: Non-disclosure can be treated as dishonesty, which is often more serious than the original offense. Talk to a lawyer about correcting it the right way.

items.q: What happens if I fail a Nevada CE audit?
items.a: Typically the board gives you a deadline to cure. Unresolved deficiencies can lead to fines or discipline.

items.q: I answered a renewal question wrong. What now?
items.a: Correct it carefully. A well-prepared correction usually goes better than the board discovering it later.

items.q: Is practicing on an expired license a big deal?
items.a: Yes. It can be treated as unlicensed practice, so stop and address it immediately.

items.q: Can I get a Nevada license with a criminal record?
items.a: Often, yes, depending on the offense, how long ago it was, and rehabilitation. Accurate disclosure is critical.

items.q: Can I appeal a Nevada license denial?
items.a: Applicants generally may request a hearing on a denial and present evidence and witnesses.

items.q: Will discipline in another state affect my Nevada application?
items.a: Yes. Nevada boards review out-of-state discipline and may impose conditions or deny.

items.q: Can a revoked Nevada license be reinstated?
items.a: Often, yes, after the required waiting period and with strong evidence of rehabilitation and competence.

items.q: How long does reinstatement take?
items.a: It varies by board and case — from a few months to longer if evaluations or hearings are required.

items.q: Can I end probation early?
items.a: Some boards allow petitions to modify or terminate probation early with good compliance.

items.q: My case was dismissed. Do I have to report it as a conviction?
items.a: Not always — but often a resolved case still involved a conviction or must be disclosed depending on the exact question. Read the question carefully and get advice before answering.

items.q: The board found an old arrest through my fingerprints. What now?
items.a: Expect questions about why the arrest happened and why it wasn't disclosed. A careful, documented explanation is essential.

items.q: Can a fraudulent application allegation lead to denial?
items.a: Yes. It can result in denial of a new license, refusal to renew, or discipline. Many cases resolve far better with early representation.

items.q: Do I have to report discipline from another state to Nevada?
items.a: Generally yes, on applications and renewals, and failure to disclose can be treated as its own violation.

items.q: Will Nevada impose the same discipline?
items.a: It may impose similar, lesser, or no additional discipline depending on the facts and your compliance with the other state's order.

items.q: Can I still get a Nevada license with prior discipline?
items.a: Often yes, sometimes with conditions. Accurate disclosure and proof of compliance are key.

items.q: Are boundary complaints public in Nevada?
items.a: Investigations are generally confidential. Formal discipline is typically public, which is why resolving a case before formal charges matters.

items.q: Can a former client's custody dispute lead to a board complaint?
items.a: Yes. Therapists and evaluators frequently receive complaints from parties in custody cases. These require a careful response that respects confidentiality rules.

items.q: Can my license be suspended immediately?
items.a: In serious cases, a board can order emergency suspension under NRS 233B.127 pending a prompt hearing.

items.q: What counts as unprofessional conduct in Nevada?
items.a: It is defined in each board's statutes and regulations and covers a wide range of behavior, from patient boundary issues to failing to collaborate with the care team.

items.q: Can a workplace conflict lead to a board complaint?
items.a: Yes. Employers and coworkers can report conduct they believe affects patient care. Context and history are critical to the defense.

items.q: Is borrowing money from a patient really a violation?
items.a: Often yes — it can be treated as exploiting the professional relationship, even if repaid.

items.q: Should I resign instead of being fired?
items.a: It depends. Resignation can still be reported, and it may affect future jobs and your board case differently. Get advice before deciding.

items.q: My employer told me to self-report. Should I?
items.a: This is a very common suggestion that needs careful discussion with an experienced attorney first. Self-reporting has real consequences.

items.q: Will my employer report me to the Nevada board?
items.a: Employers may report conduct they believe affects patient safety, including terminations. Expect a board inquiry and prepare for it.

items.q: When should I contact an attorney?
items.a: As soon as possible. You always have more options the earlier you start — and the initial consultation is free. If you've received a Notice of Investigation, the NSBN typically expects a response within 14 days.

items.q: Do I have to report an arrest to the Board?
items.a: Not always — arrests don't automatically need to be reported, but convictions must be handled carefully. Talk with an attorney before disclosing anything.

items.q: Someone from the Board called me — should I talk to them?
items.a: Be careful. Anything you say can be used against you. Consult an attorney before responding or calling back.

items.q: Can I get a revoked license back?
items.a: Often yes. After a period of time, nurses whose licenses were revoked or surrendered may pursue reinstatement. We can help you build a plan to return to practice.

items.q: What law governs the Nevada State Board of Pharmacy?
items.a: The Board of Pharmacy operates under NRS Chapter 639 and its regulations in NAC Chapter 639. Disciplinary hearings follow the Nevada Administrative Procedure Act, NRS Chapter 233B.

items.q: Does the Board of Pharmacy affect doctors and APRNs?
items.a: Yes. Physicians, physician assistants, and APRNs who dispense medications or hold a Nevada controlled substance registration can be investigated by the Board of Pharmacy, separately from their own licensing board.

items.q: What are common Board of Pharmacy complaints?
items.a: Dispensing errors, controlled-substance inventory discrepancies, diversion allegations, record-keeping violations, prescription monitoring program (PMP) issues, and impairment or substance use concerns.

items.q: What law governs the Nevada Board of Medical Examiners?
items.a: The Board of Medical Examiners licenses and disciplines MDs, physician assistants, and respiratory care practitioners under NRS Chapter 630. Grounds for discipline are listed in NRS 630.301 through 630.3065.
items.pageLabel: Nevada State Board of Medical Examiners

items.q: What happens after a complaint is filed with the Board of Medical Examiners?
items.a: A board investigator reviews the complaint and may request records or a written response. An investigative committee then decides whether to dismiss it, issue a letter of warning, or authorize a formal complaint that proceeds to a hearing under NRS Chapter 233B.
items.pageLabel: Nevada State Board of Medical Examiners

items.q: Can a malpractice lawsuit lead to a medical board investigation?
items.a: Yes. Malpractice settlements and judgments can trigger board review. Your malpractice carrier's attorney represents the civil case — your license often needs separate counsel.
items.pageLabel: Nevada State Board of Medical Examiners

items.q: What law governs the Nevada State Board of Osteopathic Medicine?
items.a: Osteopathic physicians (DOs) in Nevada are licensed and disciplined under NRS Chapter 633. Contested cases are heard under the Nevada Administrative Procedure Act, NRS Chapter 233B.
items.pageLabel: Nevada State Board of Osteopathic Medicine

items.q: Is a DO disciplined by the same board as an MD in Nevada?
items.a: No. MDs are regulated by the Board of Medical Examiners (NRS 630); DOs are regulated by the separate State Board of Osteopathic Medicine (NRS 633).
items.pageLabel: Nevada State Board of Osteopathic Medicine

items.q: What law governs the Nevada State Board of Dental Examiners?
items.a: Dentists and dental hygienists in Nevada are licensed and disciplined under NRS Chapter 631, with hearings under NRS Chapter 233B.
items.pageLabel: Nevada State Board of Dental Examiners

items.q: What complaints do Nevada dentists face?
items.a: Standard-of-care allegations, sedation and anesthesia permit issues, infection control, prescribing, advertising, and billing disputes.
items.pageLabel: Nevada State Board of Dental Examiners

items.q: What law governs chiropractors in Nevada?
items.a: Chiropractic physicians are licensed and disciplined under NRS Chapter 634, with hearings under NRS Chapter 233B.

items.q: What complaints do Nevada chiropractors face?
items.a: Billing and insurance issues, advertising violations, patient boundary allegations, and documentation problems.

items.q: What law governs the Nevada Board of Veterinary Medical Examiners?
items.a: Veterinarians and veterinary technicians in Nevada are licensed and disciplined under NRS Chapter 638, with hearings conducted under NRS Chapter 233B.
items.pageLabel: Nevada State Board of Veterinary Medical Examiners

items.q: What complaints do Nevada veterinarians face?
items.a: Allegations of negligence or substandard care, controlled-substance record-keeping, improper supervision of staff, and client communication or billing disputes.
items.pageLabel: Nevada State Board of Veterinary Medical Examiners

items.q: What law governs the Nevada Physical Therapy Board?
items.a: PTs and PTAs in Nevada are licensed and disciplined under NRS Chapter 640, with contested hearings under NRS Chapter 233B.

items.q: What complaints do Nevada physical therapists face?
items.a: Billing and documentation issues, improper supervision of PTAs or aides, boundary violations, and patient injury allegations.

items.q: What law governs occupational therapists in Nevada?
items.a: OTs and OTAs are licensed and disciplined by the Nevada Board of Occupational Therapy under NRS Chapter 640A, with hearings under NRS Chapter 233B.

items.q: What complaints do Nevada occupational therapists face?
items.a: Supervision of OTAs, billing and documentation, scope-of-practice questions, and continuing-education compliance.

items.q: What law governs psychologists in Nevada?
items.a: Psychologists are licensed and disciplined by the Nevada Board of Psychological Examiners under NRS Chapter 641, with hearings under NRS Chapter 233B.

items.q: What complaints do Nevada psychologists face?
items.a: Boundary violations, confidentiality breaches, custody-evaluation and forensic-report disputes, record-keeping, and supervision problems.

items.q: What law governs MFTs and counselors in Nevada?
items.a: Marriage and family therapists and clinical professional counselors are licensed under NRS Chapter 641A, with hearings under NRS Chapter 233B.
items.pageLabel: Nevada Board of Examiners for Marriage and Family Therapists and Clinical Professional Counselors

items.q: What complaints do Nevada therapists face?
items.a: Dual relationships, confidentiality breaches, custody-related complaints from former clients, supervision of interns, and documentation problems.
items.pageLabel: Nevada Board of Examiners for Marriage and Family Therapists and Clinical Professional Counselors

items.q: What law governs social workers in Nevada?
items.a: Social workers are licensed and disciplined by the Nevada Board of Examiners for Social Workers under NRS Chapter 641B, with hearings under NRS Chapter 233B.
items.pageLabel: Nevada Board of Examiners for Social Workers

items.q: What complaints do Nevada social workers face?
items.a: Boundary and dual-relationship allegations, confidentiality breaches, documentation problems, supervision issues, and practicing outside the scope of the license.
items.pageLabel: Nevada Board of Examiners for Social Workers

items.q: Which board licenses respiratory therapists in Nevada?
items.a: Respiratory care practitioners in Nevada are licensed and disciplined by the Nevada State Board of Medical Examiners under NRS Chapter 630.
items.pageLabel: Nevada State Board of Medical Examiners

items.q: What complaints do respiratory therapists face?
items.a: Documentation errors, medication or ventilator incidents, impairment concerns, and criminal matters that must be reported to the board.
items.pageLabel: Nevada State Board of Medical Examiners

items.q: Can ARRT discipline affect my ability to work in Nevada?
items.a: Yes. Many Nevada employers require active ARRT certification, so ARRT ethics sanctions can cost you your job even where a state license is not directly at issue.
items.pageLabel: American Registry of Radiologic Technologists (ARRT) and Nevada licensing authorities

items.q: What triggers an ARRT ethics review?
items.a: Criminal charges or convictions, employer discipline, falsified records, and failure to report a matter the ARRT requires to be reported.
items.pageLabel: American Registry of Radiologic Technologists (ARRT) and Nevada licensing authorities
